vignette:
Rabbi Mendel Cohen was 63 when he first sought help, but the roots of his distress stretched back decades to the chaotic, terrifying days of his forced displacement as a young man. He remembered the desperate scramble to escape, the guttural shouts of the border guards echoing in his ears, their rough hands pushing and pulling at the desperate crowd. He recalled the glint of a rifle butt, used to strike someone near him, and the chilling certainty that his life, and the lives of those he cherished, hung by a thread. The memory of being unexpectedly grabbed by a soldier, his arm twisted painfully, remained particularly vivid, a primal jolt that had never truly subsided.

In the aftermath, Mendel found himself haunted by an enduring sense of failure. He replayed the moments, convinced that if he had only been quicker, stronger, or somehow different, he might have averted some of the suffering he witnessed. This conviction solidified into a deep-seated belief: "I can't rely on myself," he would silently affirm, the thought a constant companion. Worse, a punishing voice within him began to insist, "I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened," feeling that his very survival was a debt he could never repay, a burden for his perceived inadequacies. His own body, too, became an adversary; even years later, in moments of calm, a sudden noise or an unexpected touch would send his heart racing, his muscles tensing, as if the danger were still imminent. "My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe," he observed, detachedly, yet with profound frustration.

Over the years, Mendel built a new life, becoming a respected Rabbi in his community, but the shadow of his past persisted, shaping his every move. He found himself constantly vigilant, a habit born of necessity during his escape. In the synagogue, he would always choose the same seat during services, positioned against a wall, facing the main entrance, a silent calculation driven by the need to feel safe and protected. This extended to his office and even his home; "I only feel safe in a very limited number of places," he realized, confining himself to familiar, controlled environments.

His daily life was a minefield of triggers. A congregant, meaning well, might place a hand on his shoulder in greeting, and Mendel would flinch internally, his whole system seizing up at the unexpected touch. The raised voice of a child during a spirited discussion in the community hall, or even a sudden burst of laughter that seemed too loud, would send a jolt through him, instantly recalling the shouts of command and chaos. Once, during a communal meal, he saw a glint of steel from a carving knife being wielded enthusiastically by a volunteer, and for a terrifying split second, his mind transported him back to the glint of the rifle, his heart hammering against his ribs.

When these moments arose, Mendel had developed various ways of coping. He would immediately try to "distract myself with something else," perhaps by focusing intently on a passage of scripture or by mentally rehearsing his next sermon, anything to pull his mind away from the terrifying sensations. However, this constant internal battle took a toll. He found himself having difficulty concentrating during his studies, during pastoral counseling, and even during prayer, his mind frequently drifting or becoming overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts.

The deep-seated belief that "somebody else would have stopped the event from happening" gnawed at him, isolating him further. This sense of personal failure, coupled with the conviction that he deserved to suffer, led him to withdraw emotionally. Despite being in a relationship, he struggled immensely with intimacy, finding it difficult to be truly emotionally close or vulnerable with his partner. He kept a part of himself guarded, fearing that if anyone truly knew the depth of his internal turmoil, they would see his weakness, his perceived failure. His partner, though loving, often expressed a longing for a deeper connection, a plea that Mendel found himself unable to fully meet. He longed for peace, for a release from the invisible chains of his past, and it was this accumulating burden, this growing chasm between him and those he loved, that finally compelled him to seek help, hoping against hope that he might yet find a way to quiet the relentless internal battle.
